headline: Iceland votes against reopening EU accession talks by 52.8% to 47.2%
dek: The result, on a turnout of about 82.5 per cent, closes the membership question for the rest of this parliament. Iceland stays inside the single market through the EEA and inside Schengen, and Brussels responded by calling it a close partner.
summary: Icelanders narrowly rejected restarting European Union accession negotiations, on a high turnout, leaving the country's existing single-market and Schengen arrangements unchanged.

image.alt: European Union flags flying in a row outside a modern government building.

body.text: Iceland has voted against reopening negotiations to join the European Union. The public broadcaster RUV's count put the No side on 52.8 per cent and the Yes side on 47.2 per cent, on a turnout of about 82.5 per cent of eligible voters, figures carried by Reuters and the Associated Press. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir's government had committed in advance to respecting the outcome.

The margin narrowed and then firmed through the night. An earlier stage of RUV's online count, reported by Al Jazeera while a handful of ballots were still outstanding in one of six constituencies, had the gap at 52.5 to 47.5. The figures in circulation are the broadcaster's tally; none of the accounts read here reported a formal certification by Iceland's electoral authorities.

The vote divided along a clear line between the capital and the rest of the country. Euronews, reporting constituency results as they came in, put Yes ahead in Reykjavik North on 57.5 per cent and in Reykjavik South on 54.5 per cent. Outside the capital the pattern reversed: No led on 60.5 per cent in the South constituency, 62.9 per cent in the Northwest and 61.2 per cent in the Northeast.

Iceland applied for membership in 2009, in the wake of its banking collapse, and a Eurosceptic government halted the negotiations in 2013, Al Jazeera reported. This referendum asked whether to pick them up again rather than whether to join, so nothing about the country's status changes as a result. Iceland remains in the European Economic Area, which gives it access to the single market, and in the Schengen travel zone.

Supporters of restarting talks pointed to relief from persistently high interest rates and to security, in the context of the war in Ukraine and American statements about Greenland, according to Al Jazeera's account of the campaign. Opponents argued that membership would cost Iceland sovereignty and control of its fishing waters.
These are not problems that Brussels will solve for us. These are problems that Icelandic politicians must solve.
body.cite: Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, opposition leader, via ABC News (Reuters/AP)

body.text: Hafsteinsdottir also said she expected the European Union to offer flexibility on fishing quotas at the outset of any negotiation, and that in her view such promises would not last. Frostadottir had said before the vote that a No would settle the question for as long as her centre-left coalition remained in office.

The European Union's response was brief and conciliatory. A European Commission spokesperson said the Commission took note of the outcome, respected the choice of the Icelandic people, and regarded Iceland as a close partner. A spokesperson for European Council President Antonio Costa said he had stressed that the EU fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic people, and described Iceland as one of the bloc's closest and most trusted partners. Costa and Frostadottir exchanged messages about strengthening relations, Euronews reported.
47% of the population was interested in it. I think it is important that we go into the coming months and weeks and respect that point of view.
body.cite: Kristrun Frostadottir, Prime Minister of Iceland, via Euronews

body.text: Frostadottir said she would not pursue membership for the remainder of her term. Euronews reported that the result is expected to shelve the question in Icelandic politics for at least two more years. Nearly half the electorate voted the other way, and the prime minister's remarks were addressed to them. Iceland remains one of a small number of Western European states outside the bloc, alongside Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, and the argument inside the country is close to evenly balanced.

body.title: What does not change
items: Iceland stays in the European Economic Area and keeps single-market access.
Iceland stays in the Schengen area.
No accession negotiation was under way; the vote was on whether to restart one.
Iceland keeps its own currency, the krona.

uncertain: The percentages and turnout are RUV's count as carried by Reuters, the Associated Press and Euronews. None of the sources read reported a formal certification by Iceland's electoral authorities.
The turnout figure of about 82.5 per cent appears in the Reuters and Associated Press account only among the sources read here.
Whether the referendum is legally binding on the government was not stated in the sources read; the government said before the vote that it would respect the result.
The final constituency-by-constituency figures, including the Southwest constituency, were still being confirmed in the reporting available.
